questions.question: What was the first commercial domain name ever registered on the internet?

answers.text: symbolics.com
apple.com
ibm.com

questions.fun_fact: Symbolics, a Massachusetts computer manufacturer, registered symbolics.com in March 1985 — beating IBM, Apple and HP to the punch. The domain still exists and was sold to an investor in 2009.

questions.question: What does the very first website ever published still describe?

answers.text: The World Wide Web project itself
A CERN particle experiment
An online phone directory

questions.fun_fact: info.cern.ch was the first website — it explained what the WWW was, how to set up a server, and how to use a browser. A restored copy is still online today.

questions.question: What was the content of the very first email ever sent over ARPANET between two computers?

answers.text: QWERTYUIOP (a test string)
Hello World
Are you receiving this?

questions.fun_fact: Ray Tomlinson, who chose the @ symbol, said the first networked email was 'something like QWERTYUIOP' — just keys mashed in a row as a test.

questions.question: Why did Ray Tomlinson choose the @ symbol for email addresses?

answers.text: It was unused in names and meant 'at'
It was the only free key on his keyboard
It was an ARPANET protocol requirement

questions.fun_fact: Tomlinson needed a separator that would never appear in someone's name. The @ key was rarely used and conveniently meant 'at' — perfect for 'user at host'.

questions.question: What was YouTube originally designed to be before it pivoted to general video sharing?

answers.text: A video dating site
A music download store
A film school portfolio site

questions.fun_fact: YouTube launched in 2005 as 'Tune In, Hook Up' — a dating site where users uploaded videos describing their ideal partner. Nobody uploaded any, so the founders opened it to all videos.

questions.question: What was the first item ever sold on eBay (then called AuctionWeb)?

answers.text: A broken laser pointer
A used Beanie Baby
A vintage comic book

questions.fun_fact: Pierre Omidyar listed a broken laser pointer for fun. It sold for $14.83. When he emailed the buyer to confirm they understood it was broken, the buyer replied: 'I'm a collector of broken laser pointers.'

questions.question: What was Amazon's original planned name before Jeff Bezos changed it?

answers.text: Cadabra
Relentless
Bookmart

questions.fun_fact: Bezos first registered Cadabra (as in 'abracadabra') — but a lawyer misheard it as 'cadaver' on the phone. He picked Amazon for the big river vibe. relentless.com still redirects to amazon.com today.

questions.question: What does the 'www' prefix on web addresses technically refer to?

answers.text: A subdomain (the web server's hostname)
A required protocol identifier
A top-level domain like .com

questions.fun_fact: 'www' is just a conventional subdomain name — like 'mail' or 'ftp'. There's no rule that web servers must use it, which is why example.com and www.example.com can serve different content.

questions.question: What was Google's original name when it was a Stanford research project?

answers.text: BackRub
PageLink
Searchly

questions.fun_fact: Larry Page and Sergey Brin called it BackRub because it analyzed 'back links' pointing to pages. They renamed it Google — a misspelling of 'googol' (10^100) — to suggest indexing huge amounts of data.

questions.question: Why does the Wi-Fi name field in routers often have a 32-character limit?

answers.text: The 802.11 SSID standard caps it at 32 bytes
Routers run out of memory beyond 32 characters
DNS rules apply to network names

questions.fun_fact: The IEEE 802.11 spec defines the SSID (Service Set Identifier) as a max 32-octet field. That hard limit predates almost every router you've ever owned.

questions.question: What did Grace Hopper's team famously tape into a logbook in 1947?

answers.text: A moth that had been stuck in a computer relay
A punch card with the very first 'Hello World' on it
A vacuum tube that had melted onto the chassis

questions.fun_fact: Operators of the Harvard Mark II found the moth jammed in a relay and labelled it 'first actual case of bug being found'. The term 'bug' for a technical fault was already decades old — Edison used it in 1878 — but the moth made the story famous. The log page is preserved at the Smithsonian.

questions.question: Why was the QWERTY keyboard layout designed the way it is?

answers.text: To space out common letters and prevent typewriter jams
To maximize typing speed for English
To match the alphabet on early telegraph keys

questions.fun_fact: Christopher Sholes arranged keys so that frequently paired letters wouldn't hit each other on mechanical typewriters. The layout stuck even after the jamming problem disappeared.

questions.question: Why is the 'save' icon in most software a floppy disk most users have never seen?

answers.text: It became a universal symbol before icons were rethought
Microsoft trademarked it and no one can change it
Floppy disks are still legally required for backups in many countries

questions.fun_fact: The 3.5-inch floppy became the 'save' icon in the 1980s and stuck around through inertia. A whole generation now recognizes the symbol without ever having touched the object.

questions.question: What does the 'Ctrl+Alt+Delete' shortcut on Windows actually do at the hardware level?

answers.text: Triggers a secure interrupt the OS reserves for itself
Sends three simultaneous keypresses to any focused app
Cuts power to the keyboard controller

questions.fun_fact: Originally an IBM PC engineer's debugging shortcut for quick reboots, the combo was repurposed as a 'Secure Attention Sequence' so malware couldn't fake the Windows login screen.

questions.question: Why do file paths on Windows use backslashes while almost every other OS uses forward slashes?

answers.text: DOS already used forward slash for command options
Microsoft wanted to differentiate from Unix on principle
Backslash was the only key not used by IBM PC software

questions.fun_fact: MS-DOS used / for command flags before it gained directories. When subfolders were added, the / was taken — so Microsoft picked \ for paths, and Windows inherited it forever.

questions.question: What does the 'K' in 'OK button' historically stand for in some accounts?

answers.text: A joking misspelling of 'all correct' (oll korrect)
The German word 'klar' meaning clear
Kelvin, used in early thermal acknowledgments

questions.fun_fact: OK likely comes from 1830s Boston newspaper slang where misspellings were a running joke — 'oll korrect' was abbreviated OK. It became one of the most universal words on Earth.

questions.question: Why does the loading 'hourglass' or 'spinner' often spin even when nothing is happening?

answers.text: It's animated on a separate thread, decoupled from real work
It's tied to CPU clock cycles, not actual progress
Operating systems require visible animation at all times

questions.fun_fact: Spinners usually run on a UI thread independent of the task. If the worker crashes or hangs, the animation keeps going — giving the illusion of progress when there is none.

questions.question: What is the origin of the term 'spam' for unwanted email?

answers.text: A Monty Python sketch where Spam dominates a menu
An acronym for 'Sending Persistent Annoying Mail'
A bug in an early IBM mail server called SPAM-1

questions.fun_fact: In the sketch, every dish on the menu contains Spam and Vikings drown out conversation chanting 'spam, spam, spam'. Early online users started using it for messages that drowned out discussion.

questions.question: Why is computer memory measured in bytes of 8 bits, not 10?

answers.text: 8 bits cleanly encode one character in early systems
The first transistor packs had exactly 8 pins
Binary math only works with multiples of 8

questions.fun_fact: IBM's System/360 in the 1960s standardized 8-bit bytes because that was enough to encode every character plus some control codes. The choice locked in for the next 60 years of computing.

questions.question: What does CAPTCHA literally stand for?

answers.text: Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart
Common Access Protocol To Counter Hostile Automation
Centralized Authentication Process for Trusted Human Access

questions.fun_fact: Coined at Carnegie Mellon in 2003, the acronym is a nod to Alan Turing's test. ReCAPTCHA was later used by Google to help digitize old books — every squiggly word you typed trained their OCR.

questions.question: Why is Bluetooth named after a medieval Viking king?

answers.text: Harald 'Bluetooth' united Denmark — symbolizing unified devices
His tomb was found near the inventor's home in Lund
His face appeared on Ericsson's first wireless chip

questions.fun_fact: King Harald Blåtand united Danish tribes around 958. Intel engineer Jim Kardach proposed the name for a tech that 'unites' devices. The Bluetooth logo is even a rune monogram of his initials H and B.

questions.question: Wi-Fi research at CSIRO drew from work originally aimed at detecting what?

answers.text: Exploding mini black holes in radio astronomy
Soviet submarine sonar signatures
Atmospheric lightning strikes for weather modeling

questions.fun_fact: Australian astronomer John O'Sullivan worked on math to clean up radio signals from evaporating black holes. The technique was repurposed at CSIRO into the algorithms behind 802.11a/g Wi-Fi.

questions.question: What was the first widely-sold USB flash drive's storage capacity at launch?

answers.text: 8 megabytes
128 megabytes
512 kilobytes

questions.fun_fact: IBM and Trek 2000 launched the DiskOnKey / ThumbDrive around 2000 at 8 MB — roughly five floppy disks' worth — and it instantly replaced the floppy in offices worldwide.

questions.question: Why does the iPhone's default keyboard show a '123' key instead of a number row?

answers.text: To keep letters big enough for fat-finger accuracy
Apple patented the modal layout and forbade number rows
iOS can't render two keyboard rows above the spacebar

questions.fun_fact: Apple's HCI team found that adding a number row shrank letter keys enough to push typo rates noticeably higher. The modal '123' layout was a deliberate accuracy tradeoff.

questions.question: Why do many TV remotes still send infrared light instead of using Bluetooth?

answers.text: Infrared is cheap, low-power and good enough for one-way commands
Bluetooth signals interfere with TV tuners
FCC rules forbid radio remotes for home electronics

questions.fun_fact: An IR LED and a button cell can outlive the TV. Bluetooth needs pairing, more power, and more silicon. For 'press button → channel changes', IR remains hard to beat economically.

questions.question: What was the original purpose of the SD card's tiny write-protect switch?

answers.text: Purely a hint — the host device decides whether to honor it
A hardware fuse that physically blocks the write pin
A backup power switch for the internal controller

questions.fun_fact: The lock tab does nothing inside the card. It just flips a switch in the slot the host reads. Any device — or any tape covering the switch — can ignore it completely.

questions.question: Why do car key fobs occasionally stop working in supermarket parking lots?

answers.text: Nearby radio noise can jam their weak signal
Steel shopping carts block the signal entirely
Car batteries detect crowds and disable remote unlock

questions.fun_fact: Car remotes use unlicensed bands shared with other devices. Old freezer compressors, broken LED signs, even other cars' transmitters can blanket a parking lot in noise until you walk closer to your car.

questions.question: Why was the original Game Boy screen green?

answers.text: Cheap reflective LCDs rendered best in green
Nintendo's mascot Mario wore green at the time
Green light is less harmful to children's eyes

questions.fun_fact: Nintendo picked a reflective monochrome LCD to maximize battery life. The cheapest, highest-contrast option happened to render in that famous swampy green.

questions.question: Why does the Roomba sometimes spiral instead of going straight?

answers.text: It uses random-walk algorithms instead of a map
It's tracking a hidden ceiling beacon
It calibrates its gyroscope every few minutes

questions.fun_fact: Early Roombas had no SLAM mapping. They used a mix of straight runs, wall-following, and spirals on dirty spots — descended from MIT robotics research on simple insect-like behaviors.

questions.question: Why did early digital cameras include a fake 'click' shutter sound?

answers.text: To reassure users the picture was actually taken
FCC rules required an audible operation signal
It masked the sound of writing data to memory cards

questions.fun_fact: Without moving mirrors, digital cameras are silent. Designers added the synthetic click for confidence — and in Japan and South Korea, regulators later required it to deter surreptitious photos.

questions.question: Why did the supersonic Concorde get noticeably longer during flight?

answers.text: Friction heating stretched the airframe by about 20 cm
Wing flex pulled the fuselage like a rubber band
Fuel transfer extended an internal telescoping section

questions.fun_fact: At Mach 2, skin temperatures hit ~100°C and the aluminum airframe expanded. Pilots would wedge their cap into a gap between panels during cruise; on landing the gap closed again, trapping it.

questions.question: What was the very first item to be sold over the internet according to one well-known account?

answers.text: A Sting CD on a site called NetMarket
A pepperoni pizza from Pizza Hut
A Stanford-branded coffee mug

questions.fun_fact: In August 1994, NetMarket sold a Sting CD over an SSL-encrypted connection — the first widely-publicized secure online purchase. The New York Times wrote about it the next day.

questions.question: Why do commercial airliners dim the cabin lights for takeoff and landing at night?

answers.text: So eyes adapt to the dark if an evacuation is needed
To reduce strain on the engines' generators
Because dim lights help passengers sleep faster

questions.fun_fact: If something goes wrong on takeoff or landing — the riskiest phases — your eyes are already adjusted to outside darkness, so you can see emergency lighting and exits the moment you stand up.

questions.question: Why do car cup holders exist in such ridiculous numbers in American cars?

answers.text: The drive-through coffee culture pushed automakers to add more
US federal safety rules mandate one per seat
Insurance premiums dropped for cars with more holders

questions.fun_fact: Cup holders only became standard after the 1980s as fast-food and giant sodas exploded. Today some minivans have 18+ cup holders — a number that bewilders European designers.

questions.question: Tesla cars famously hide a 'Mars' easter egg in which interface?

answers.text: The navigation map, which can switch to a Martian surface view
The seat-massage menu, which has a 'Mars gravity' setting
The charging screen, which shows a SpaceX rocket fueling

questions.fun_fact: After the Falcon Heavy launched a Tesla Roadster toward Mars, Tesla added a software toggle that re-skins the navigation map as the surface of Mars — a nod to Elon Musk's other company.

questions.question: Why are airplane windows always rounded instead of square?

answers.text: Square corners concentrate stress and crack the fuselage
Round windows are cheaper to manufacture
They prevent reflections that disorient pilots

questions.fun_fact: The de Havilland Comet, the first jet airliner, had square windows. Several broke up mid-flight when metal fatigue cracked from the corners. Every airliner since has used rounded windows.

questions.question: Why does the steering wheel of most modern cars vibrate when you drift out of your lane?

answers.text: A motor mimics a rumble strip via the steering column
The tires actually detect lane paint under them
The brake assist briefly grabs one wheel

questions.fun_fact: Lane-keep systems use cameras to spot lane lines, then drive a small motor in the steering column to fake the feel of a rumble strip — taking advantage of a reflex drivers already know.

questions.question: What is unusual about the toilet flush on a commercial airliner?

answers.text: It uses vacuum suction, not water flow
It heats waste to over 200°C before storing it
It dumps waste into a sealed compartment in the wing

questions.fun_fact: Aircraft toilets use a partial vacuum, so a tiny squirt of non-stick coating and a blast of air whisks waste into a tank. Modern planes do not — contrary to legend — dump it in flight.

questions.question: Why do many Boeing 747s historically carry a small spiral staircase in the front?

answers.text: To reach the upper deck, originally a first-class lounge
It's a structural reinforcement disguised as stairs
It hides the cockpit emergency exit hatch

questions.fun_fact: The 747's upper deck began life as a piano bar / lounge for first-class passengers in the 1970s. The famous spiral staircase led up to it — later airlines replaced it with seats.

questions.question: Why do modern cars often play an artificial engine sound through the speakers?

answers.text: Quiet engines feel underpowered, so the sound is faked
Regulations require a minimum engine volume inside the cabin
It's a side effect of active noise cancellation

questions.fun_fact: Many turbocharged and electric cars are so quiet that drivers feel disconnected. Manufacturers like BMW, Ford and VW pipe synthesized engine sound through the speakers to restore the feel of speed.

questions.question: Why did Amazon Alexa devices once start ordering dollhouses across an entire US city?

answers.text: A TV anchor said the trigger phrase on the news
A firmware bug looped a sample order command
Children figured out a shared voice exploit

questions.fun_fact: In 2017, a San Diego morning show reported on a girl who'd ordered a dollhouse via Alexa. The anchor repeated the phrase on air — and Alexas in countless living rooms tried to order their own.

questions.question: Why does the Roomba have an origin in military robotics?

answers.text: iRobot first built bomb-disposal and reconnaissance robots
DARPA funded the original vacuum prototype
It was reverse-engineered from a Soviet floor-cleaning drone

questions.fun_fact: iRobot built the PackBot, used in Iraq and Afghanistan for bomb disposal, before they made the Roomba. Cleaning floors and clearing IEDs share more navigation challenges than you'd think.

questions.question: Why did early Google Home devices sometimes wake up during Super Bowl ads?

answers.text: The ads contained the wake phrase 'OK Google'
TV audio briefly exceeded a frequency threshold
Cellphone signals during the game spoofed the trigger

questions.fun_fact: A 2017 Google Home Super Bowl ad triggered every Google Home within earshot of a TV. Google had to detect its own ad audio and filter it — and other voice assistants now do the same.

questions.question: Why are smart light bulbs sometimes a major home security risk?

answers.text: Discarded bulbs can leak stored Wi-Fi credentials
They run a full Linux kernel exposed to the internet
Their LEDs leak the home's MAC address as light flicker

questions.fun_fact: Researchers have pulled plaintext Wi-Fi passwords from used smart bulbs bought on eBay. The cheap microcontrollers inside often store credentials unencrypted in flash memory.

questions.question: Why do many smart speakers occasionally answer a question nobody asked?

answers.text: Background audio briefly resembles the wake word
They periodically test their own speech engine out loud
Their microphones pick up the neighbor's speaker as a signal

questions.fun_fact: Wake-word detection is tuned to favor false positives over missed activations. TV dialogue, certain song lyrics, even a slammed door can sound enough like 'Alexa' or 'Hey Google' to wake the device.

questions.question: Why was the term 'thermostat war' coined in some smart-home households?

answers.text: Multiple smart thermostats overriding each other in loops
AI assistants arguing over preferred room temperature
A patent dispute between Nest and Ecobee

questions.fun_fact: Households with HomeKit, Nest and Alexa-integrated thermostats have reported feedback loops where each platform 'corrects' the other's setting, leaving the heater oscillating all night.

questions.question: Why does Microsoft's Tay chatbot remain a famous AI cautionary tale?

answers.text: Twitter users taught it offensive opinions within 24 hours
It tried to phone the police on a Microsoft engineer
It accidentally started a flame war with Cortana

questions.fun_fact: Released in 2016, Tay learned from public Twitter interactions. Trolls coordinated to flood it with abusive content, and Microsoft pulled the bot offline less than a day later.

questions.question: Why are some robot vacuums banned from certain government buildings?

answers.text: They map floor plans and upload them to the cloud
Their LIDAR interferes with security cameras
Their batteries fail safety standards

questions.fun_fact: Several agencies have raised concerns that cloud-connected robot vacuums build detailed maps of building interiors. For sensitive sites, that's a counterintelligence problem.

questions.question: Why did some smart fridges in 2014 reportedly send spam emails?

answers.text: They were hijacked into a botnet via weak credentials
They auto-emailed grocery lists to whole address books
A firmware bug attached marketing PDFs to every email

questions.fun_fact: Security firm Proofpoint reported that compromised IoT devices — including at least one internet-connected fridge — sent hundreds of thousands of spam emails as part of a botnet.

questions.question: Why do many AI image generators struggle to draw human hands correctly?

answers.text: Hands appear in countless poses in training data
Their training data deliberately excludes hand close-ups
The models can't process more than four fingers per object

questions.fun_fact: Hands take wildly different shapes from every angle, fingers overlap, and training images label them inconsistently. Models often produce a 'hand-shaped blob' with the wrong finger count.

questions.question: What was the ENIAC computer's primary original purpose when built during World War II?

answers.text: Calculating artillery firing tables
Breaking the German Enigma code
Simulating early atomic-bomb yields

questions.fun_fact: ENIAC was commissioned by the US Army's Ballistic Research Laboratory to crunch firing tables that human 'computers' couldn't keep up with. By the time it was operational in 1945, the war was almost over — so its first real workloads were hydrogen-bomb feasibility calculations.

questions.question: Why did early programmers refer to computer operators as 'computers' themselves?

answers.text: 'Computer' originally meant a person who did calculations by hand
Operators wore lab coats matching the machine's color
Each operator was assigned a serial number like the machines

questions.fun_fact: Until the 1940s, a 'computer' was a job title — often held by women who did long arithmetic for astronomy, physics or ballistics. The electronic machine was named after them, not the other way around.

questions.question: Why was the world's first stored-program computer nicknamed 'Baby'?

answers.text: It was a small test machine for a larger planned successor
Its inventors' newborn daughter inspired the name
It cried out an audible tone whenever it crashed

questions.fun_fact: The Manchester Baby ran its first program in June 1948 — 52 minutes to find the highest factor of a number. It was a small-scale proof-of-concept for the larger Manchester Mark 1.

questions.question: What was unusual about the Apollo Guidance Computer's memory compared to modern RAM?

answers.text: It was woven by hand from copper wire and tiny ferrite cores
It used vacuum tubes the size of a deck of cards
It stored data magnetically on punched paper tape

questions.fun_fact: The AGC's read-only program memory was 'core rope' — wires threaded by hand through or around tiny iron rings to encode 1s and 0s. The work was done by women at Raytheon, sometimes called 'Little Old Lady' memory.

questions.question: Why did early hard disks make a loud clunking sound when powered off?

answers.text: The read/write head physically parked itself against a stop
Internal capacitors discharged through the chassis
The cooling fan slammed shut to seal out dust

questions.fun_fact: Old drives moved the head with a solenoid that snapped it to a parking position when power was cut. Modern drives use a gentler ramp, but the iconic 'clunk' lives on in retro-computing nostalgia.

questions.question: Why did punch cards have one corner clipped off diagonally?

answers.text: So operators could see at a glance if a card was misaligned
To fit them through narrow card-reader slots
To reserve a spot for the operator's initials

questions.fun_fact: A dropped deck was an operator's nightmare. The clipped corner — combined with diagonal stripes drawn across the deck's edge — let you spot upside-down or out-of-order cards instantly.

questions.question: What did the Xerox Alto, built in 1973, pioneer that wouldn't reach the public for nearly a decade?

answers.text: A graphical user interface with mouse and windows
Color laser printing in the home
Touchscreen tablet input

questions.fun_fact: The Alto had a bitmapped display, a three-button mouse, overlapping windows and Ethernet networking — years before Apple's Lisa or the Macintosh. Steve Jobs famously visited Xerox PARC in 1979 and was floored.

questions.question: Why are floppy disks called 'floppy' if the 3.5-inch ones felt rigid?

answers.text: The magnetic disk inside the hard plastic shell is flexible
The earliest prototypes folded in half for storage
Engineers named them after a cartoon character

questions.fun_fact: Open a 3.5-inch floppy and you'll find a thin, bendy magnetic disk inside. The 5.25-inch and 8-inch ancestors had no rigid shell at all — those were genuinely floppy.

questions.question: Why did IBM choose Microsoft's DOS over its main rival CP/M for the original IBM PC?

answers.text: CP/M's author missed the crucial meeting with IBM
CP/M cost ten times as much per license
CP/M didn't support IBM's new floppy format

questions.fun_fact: The legend goes that Digital Research's Gary Kildall was flying his plane the day IBM came calling, and the deal slipped to Microsoft — who didn't even own a DOS yet and quickly bought QDOS to relicense. Historians dispute the details, but the missed-meeting story is enshrined in tech lore.

questions.question: What did the very first webcam ever made monitor, sitting in a Cambridge University break room?

answers.text: A coffee pot, so researchers knew when it was full
A fish tank, as a screen-saver experiment
A whiteboard, to share notes between offices

questions.fun_fact: The Trojan Room Coffee Pot at Cambridge's Computer Lab was the first webcam subject — set up in 1991 so people upstairs didn't trudge down to an empty pot. It went online in 1993 and ran until 2001.

questions.question: Why is the file-format extension '.zip' named that way?

answers.text: To suggest the speed of compressing files compared to ARC
It abbreviates 'Zero-Information Packaging'
Its creator's wife was nicknamed Zippy

questions.fun_fact: Phil Katz designed PKZIP in 1989 as a faster competitor to the dominant ARC format. He picked 'zip' for the sound of moving quickly. The format has outlived almost every other compressor of its era.

questions.question: What did the world's first banner ad in 1994 advertise?

answers.text: AT&T's vision of the future internet
Netscape's brand-new web browser
Pizza Hut's online ordering trial

questions.fun_fact: HotWired ran the AT&T ad in October 1994 with the line 'Have you ever clicked your mouse right HERE?'. Its click-through rate was a now-unimaginable 44%.

questions.question: Why does the HTTP status code '418' exist in the official IETF specification?

answers.text: It's an April Fools' joke: 'I'm a teapot'
It signals that a server is over its hourly request quota
It identifies servers reserved for academic use only

questions.fun_fact: RFC 2324, published on April 1, 1998, defined the Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol. Teapots are supposed to refuse to brew coffee with status 418 — and several real web frameworks support it for fun.

questions.question: What is the original meaning of the term 'cookie' in web browsers?

answers.text: Borrowed from 'magic cookie' — a token passed between programs
An acronym for 'Client-Owned Object Key'
Named after Cookie Monster as a Netscape inside joke

questions.fun_fact: Unix programs had been passing 'magic cookies' — opaque tokens of state — long before the web existed. Netscape's Lou Montulli borrowed the term in 1994 for the tiny files browsers stored on disk.

questions.question: Why does the typical URL include the cryptic-looking sequence '://'?

answers.text: Tim Berners-Lee later said he wished he had skipped it
It's required by the TCP/IP packet format
Each character signals a different routing layer

questions.fun_fact: Berners-Lee has apologised in talks for the '//' in URLs — he admitted it wasn't strictly necessary and that the world would have saved an enormous amount of typing if he'd left it out.

questions.question: What was the first phone widely sold as a 'smartphone' before the iPhone?

answers.text: The IBM Simon Personal Communicator
The original Palm Pilot
The Nokia 3310

questions.fun_fact: IBM Simon launched in 1994 — a brick with a touchscreen, email, fax, calendar and apps. Only about 50,000 sold, but it predates the term 'smartphone' becoming common by nearly a decade.

questions.question: Why did early iPhone cameras lack a flash for the first three generations?

answers.text: Apple judged early LED flashes too ugly and too power-hungry
Patents from Nokia blocked use of LED flashes on phones
Apple was waiting for a flash thin enough to fit

questions.fun_fact: The flash didn't arrive until the iPhone 4 in 2010. Apple was famously reluctant to ship hardware they considered low-quality, preferring no feature to a bad one.

questions.question: Why does the modern smartphone touchscreen typically not work with a regular pencil eraser?

answers.text: It senses the tiny electrical charge of a fingertip, not pressure
Erasers are slightly too small to register
The pencil graphite confuses the optical sensors

questions.fun_fact: Capacitive touchscreens detect changes in a tiny electrical field at the surface. Rubber erasers don't conduct, so they're invisible — but a banana, a sausage or a damp glove will all happily tap a phone.

questions.question: Why do most smartphones use 'lithium-polymer' instead of removable AA-style batteries?

answers.text: Polymer batteries can be molded into thin custom shapes
AA cells don't hold a charge long enough for any phone
Polymer cells are the only kind that can fast-charge

questions.fun_fact: Lithium-polymer cells use a flexible pouch instead of a rigid can, so designers can shape them around cameras and antennas. That's why a modern phone has a strange-looking battery you can't easily swap.

questions.question: Why do mobile phone signals weaken inside elevators and basements?

answers.text: Metal walls form a 'Faraday cage' that blocks radio waves
Network operators throttle service in enclosed spaces
Building electrical wiring cancels cell-tower frequencies

questions.fun_fact: A continuous metal shell traps radio waves on its outer surface, leaving a quiet zone inside. The same physics is why a car can be safe in a lightning storm and why your microwave doesn't cook you.

questions.question: Why did 19th-century umbrella makers go to court when steel ribs replaced whalebone ribs?

answers.text: Whalebone-rib patents tried to block the cheaper steel ones
Steel ribs were declared dangerous in lightning storms
Whaling unions sued to keep their bone supply contracts

questions.fun_fact: Samuel Fox patented his steel 'Paragon' umbrella frame in 1852, but earlier whalebone patent holders fought to keep their market. Steel won, and whales got a small early reprieve as a side effect.

questions.question: Why are most modern bicycle chains 'half-inch pitch'?

answers.text: An early standard from the 1880s that everyone copied
It's the smallest pitch that survives off-road use
Half-inch matches the wheel rim's bead-seat diameter

questions.fun_fact: The half-inch (12.7 mm) pitch was set by early bicycle and roller-chain makers in Britain. It became so widespread that gear teeth, derailleurs and chainrings worldwide are still built around it — even on $10,000 racing bikes.

questions.question: Why does a Phillips-head screw deliberately let the screwdriver slip out under high torque?

answers.text: To prevent over-tightening on early assembly lines
To stop the screw head from snapping off
To make removal easier years later when rusted

questions.fun_fact: Henry Phillips' cross-shaped slot was designed to 'cam out' before stripping the screw or breaking the joint — useful when factory torque wrenches were rare. Modern variants like Pozidriv reduce that effect.

questions.question: Why do most modern can openers cut the side of the can instead of the lid?

answers.text: It leaves a smoother edge and no metal slivers in the food
It uses less force, easier on arthritic hands
It's a regulatory requirement in the EU

questions.fun_fact: Side-cutting 'safety' openers separate the rim from the can wall, leaving the lid as a non-sharp disc that lifts out. The classic top-cutting design left a jagged ring and tiny metal shavings — a hidden food-safety issue.

questions.question: Why does a Thermos flask keep both hot drinks hot and cold drinks cold?

answers.text: A vacuum gap blocks heat from flowing in or out
Its lining absorbs the dominant temperature of its contents
An internal heat exchanger averages the temperature both ways

questions.fun_fact: James Dewar's 1892 vacuum flask removes nearly all the air between two glass walls, killing conduction and convection. Heat can only escape by radiation, which the silver coating reflects back.

questions.question: Why do railway tracks usually have a small gap between sections of rail?

answers.text: Steel expands in hot weather and would buckle otherwise
It's where the signalling sensors connect to the rail
Each gap marks the end of one rail-owner's section

questions.fun_fact: Steel rails grow several centimetres per kilometre on hot summer days. The classic 'clickety-clack' sound was the wheels crossing those expansion gaps. Continuous welded rail today uses prestressing instead.

questions.question: Why do commercial jet engines often have spiral patterns painted on their spinning hubs?

answers.text: To make it obvious from outside whether the engine is running
To improve airflow into the compressor blades
To reduce icing through a strobe effect

questions.fun_fact: Ground crews need a quick visual check before approaching an engine, since a running turbofan can suck in a person from many metres away. The spiral becomes a blurred disc when the engine is spooled up.

questions.question: Why is the maximum length of a freight train in many countries limited by air-brake physics?

answers.text: Brake-line pressure takes too long to reach the last cars
Steel couplers can't take the pull of more than 100 cars
Diesel engines run out of fuel beyond a fixed length

questions.fun_fact: Westinghouse-style air brakes work by venting pressure along a single hose. On very long trains, the rear cars react seconds later than the front, risking jackknifing — which is why distributed locomotives in the middle of the train help.

questions.question: Why are most car license plates in Europe roughly the same size?

answers.text: An EU directive standardised the dimensions in the 1990s
Plate makers across Europe share a single supplier
Speed cameras can only read one specific plate size

questions.fun_fact: The EU's standard plate (520×110 mm) lets cars cross borders without swapping plates and gives speed cameras a predictable target. Some countries — like the UK — also allow a taller two-row variant.

questions.question: Why are diesel locomotives almost always actually 'diesel-electric'?

answers.text: The diesel engine runs a generator that powers electric motors
Diesel engines can't reverse direction quickly enough on their own
Pure diesel locomotives are banned in most countries

questions.fun_fact: Mechanically connecting a diesel engine to the wheels of a heavy train would need a monstrous gearbox. Instead, the engine spins a generator, and electric traction motors at each axle do the work — high torque from zero RPM, no clutch.

questions.question: Why do many airliners have a small upturned 'winglet' at the wingtips?

answers.text: It reduces the swirling vortex that wastes fuel
It's required as a navigation-light mounting point
It stops birds from striking the wing edge

questions.fun_fact: High-pressure air under the wing leaks around to the low-pressure top, forming a vortex that drags the plane backward. Winglets disrupt that leak, saving roughly 4–5% of fuel on a long flight.

questions.question: Why do most modern wind turbines have exactly three blades?

answers.text: Three blades balance efficiency, cost and smooth rotation
Two-blade designs are forbidden by aviation authorities
Three matches the number of phases in the power grid

questions.fun_fact: More blades catch slightly more wind but cost more and create more drag; two blades are cheaper but vibrate as they pass the tower. Three is the engineering sweet spot — and looks more pleasing to most people, too.

questions.question: Why do pumped-storage hydro plants count as 'giant batteries' for the grid?

answers.text: They pump water uphill when power is cheap and release it when needed
They store electricity in supercapacitors lining the dam wall
Their turbines double as chemical battery banks

questions.fun_fact: Excess solar or wind power runs giant pumps that lift water into an upper reservoir. When demand spikes, the water rushes back down through turbines — round-trip efficiency around 70–80%. It's still the dominant grid-scale energy storage on Earth.

questions.question: Why do modern home LED bulbs often have a small 'brick' attached at the base?

answers.text: It converts mains AC into the low-voltage DC the LED needs
It is a tiny battery that smooths flicker during power dips
It is an antenna for the bulb's smart-home features

questions.fun_fact: An LED needs steady DC at a few volts, but your wall socket delivers fluctuating AC at 120 or 230 V. The little driver brick crammed into the screw base handles the conversion — and is often the first thing to fail.

questions.question: Why does a single nuclear fuel pellet the size of a fingertip contain so much energy?

answers.text: Splitting uranium releases millions of times more energy than burning coal
Each pellet is compressed under extreme pressure before use
The pellet is filled with liquid hydrogen as a booster

questions.fun_fact: One uranium-235 fission releases about 200 million electron-volts; burning a carbon atom releases about 4. A pellet the size of a pencil eraser can match the energy of about a tonne of coal.

questions.question: Why is Gorilla Glass on smartphones so much tougher than ordinary window glass?

answers.text: It is dunked in molten salt to swap small ions for larger ones
It is laminated with an invisible layer of woven Kevlar
It is annealed for several days in a vacuum oven

questions.fun_fact: Corning's process puts the glass in a 400 °C potassium salt bath. Larger potassium ions squeeze into spots vacated by smaller sodium ones, leaving the surface under permanent compression — like prestressed concrete.

questions.question: Why is graphene considered a 'wonder material' in modern research?

answers.text: It is a one-atom-thick sheet of carbon stronger than steel
It is the only known room-temperature superconductor
It can fold and unfold itself when heated

questions.fun_fact: Graphene was first isolated in 2004 by peeling layers off graphite with sticky tape — a trick that won the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics. A square metre weighs less than a milligram but supports the weight of a cat.

questions.question: Why does a memory-foam mattress feel firmer in a cold room than in a warm one?

answers.text: Its polymer becomes more rigid as temperature drops
The air pockets inside shrink and the foam compresses less
Cold air increases friction between the foam cells

questions.fun_fact: Memory foam is a viscoelastic polyurethane: warmer temperatures soften it and let it mould to the body, cooler ones stiffen it. NASA originally developed the material to cushion astronauts during launch.

questions.question: Why are bulletproof vests usually built from many thin layers instead of one thick sheet?

answers.text: Each layer absorbs and spreads a bit of the bullet's energy
Single sheets crack instantly under any impact
Manufacturing limits prevent making thicker sheets

questions.fun_fact: Layers of woven Kevlar or UHMWPE catch the bullet like a net, stretching and decelerating it across the whole vest. A solid plate would still stop the bullet, but transfer far more bruising force to the wearer.

questions.question: Why does a typical fingerprint sensor on a phone work even if your finger is slightly dirty?

answers.text: It senses tiny electrical capacitance differences between ridges and valleys
It scans body heat through the glass cover
It uses ultrasound to image the bone underneath

questions.fun_fact: Capacitive fingerprint sensors don't take a 'photo' — they map a grid of tiny capacitors that respond differently to the skin ridges and the air gaps between them. Some newer phones do use ultrasound to image deeper.

questions.question: Why does an ABS car-brake sensor at each wheel use a small toothed ring?

answers.text: A magnetic sensor counts the teeth to measure wheel speed
The teeth physically vibrate the brake to prevent lockup
The teeth dissipate heat from the brake disc

questions.fun_fact: The toothed 'tone ring' spins past a magnetic pickup, producing a frequency proportional to wheel speed. Anti-lock brakes compare wheels and release pressure on any wheel about to lock — too fast for a human to do.

questions.question: Why does a passive infrared (PIR) motion sensor often miss a person standing perfectly still?

answers.text: It detects changes in heat across its field, not absolute heat
Its sensor needs ultrasonic input to confirm the signal
Standing humans emit less heat than walking ones

questions.fun_fact: A PIR sensor's two halves see the world through a segmented lens. When a warm body moves across the segments, the two halves see unequal heat and trigger. A motionless person produces no difference — and goes unseen.

questions.question: Why do tall skyscrapers usually sway a noticeable amount in the wind?

answers.text: A flexible structure absorbs wind energy better than a rigid one
It saves on steel by allowing some movement
Sway is required to keep elevators balanced

questions.fun_fact: Skyscrapers are designed to flex — sometimes a metre or more at the top — so the wind's energy is dissipated instead of shattering rigid joints. The Taipei 101 even has a huge tuned mass damper hanging inside to soak up the motion.

questions.question: Why is concrete usually reinforced with steel bars inside?

answers.text: Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension
Steel keeps the concrete from drying too fast
The bars conduct away electrical surges during storms

questions.fun_fact: Squeeze concrete and it shrugs you off; pull it apart and it cracks easily. Steel bars handle the pulling forces — and conveniently expand and contract at almost the same rate as concrete, so they don't crack the slab in temperature swings.

questions.question: Why are large suspension bridges almost always cleaned and painted continuously?

answers.text: Rust would slowly weaken the steel cables and deck
Paint refreshes the bridge's radar signature for aviation
Inspections legally require visible new paint each year

questions.fun_fact: The Golden Gate Bridge's iconic 'international orange' is constantly being touched up — a small crew has been painting it nearly nonstop since 1937. The aim is not aesthetics but corrosion protection.

questions.question: Why did the Morris Worm of 1988 inadvertently bring down much of the early internet?

answers.text: A bug made it infect each machine many times, overloading it
It deliberately deleted system files on every host
It cut transatlantic cables by attacking router firmware

questions.fun_fact: Robert Morris meant to gauge the size of the internet, not crash it — but his worm reinfected machines repeatedly, grinding them to a halt. He became the first person convicted under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.

questions.question: Why are passwords typically stored as 'hashes' rather than as plain text?

answers.text: A stolen hash file does not reveal the original passwords
Hashes take less disk space than passwords
Hashes are required by law in most countries

questions.fun_fact: A good hash function turns a password into a fixed-length scramble that can't be reversed. The site only stores the hash and re-hashes what you type to compare. Even an attacker who steals the database has to guess each password and rehash.

questions.question: Why was the Linux operating system originally announced as 'just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu'?

answers.text: Linus Torvalds posted that line on a Usenet group in 1991
It was Richard Stallman's review of an early Linux release
Bell Labs added it as a footnote to a Unix manual

questions.fun_fact: Torvalds, then a student in Helsinki, modestly underestimated his project in his August 1991 announcement on comp.os.minix. Today, Linux runs most servers, all of Android, and every one of the world's fastest supercomputers.

questions.question: Why does the open-source license 'BSD' have so many slightly different versions?

answers.text: Various clauses were dropped over time as legally unnecessary
Each US university wanted its own variant
International translations changed the legal meaning

questions.fun_fact: The original BSD license had four clauses, including an 'advertising clause' requiring every ad to credit Berkeley. Over the years projects trimmed it down — modern 2-clause and 3-clause BSD are the survivors.

questions.question: Why does the Mozilla Firefox browser have a fox wrapped around a globe as its logo?

answers.text: The name refers to a red panda — sometimes called a 'firefox'
Mozilla wanted a wild-animal logo for every product
An early intern's pet fox inspired the original sketch

questions.fun_fact: The Firefox name is the English nickname for the red panda. Mozilla later sponsored two real red pandas at Knoxville Zoo. The logo is sometimes mistaken for a regular fox, but the project has always meant the panda.
